title: Sedimentary Rocks & Weathering
intro: First weathering (how rock breaks down, and how soil forms), then sedimentary rocks (how the pieces become layered rock and what the layers tell us).

learningObjectives.text: Explain how water drives weathering and transports sediment.
Compare physical and chemical weathering and explain how surface area affects weathering rate.
Identify mechanical weathering processes and explain how they break rock apart.
Explain chemical weathering and how it produces differential weathering.
Explain how climate and parent material affect soil formation and soil horizons.
Classify soils using their horizons and the criteria covered in the lesson.
Define sediment and distinguish clastic, biochemical, organic, and chemical sedimentary rocks.
Explain how clastic sedimentary rocks form and classify them by grain size, sorting, and composition.
Distinguish biochemical, organic, and chemical sedimentary rocks by how they form.
Identify bedding, formations, and common sedimentary structures in rock exposures.
Relate depositional environments to the sedimentary features of deltas.
Explain how basins, sea-level change, and facies relate to sediment deposition.

boxes.text: Why does freezing break rock? Water seeps into a crack. When it turns to ice it needs MORE room, so it pushes the crack wider with huge force. When it melts, liquid water flows deeper into the wider crack. Repeat many times and the rock splits.
Think of a full bottle of water left in the freezer: the bottle cracks. A crack in rock is the bottle.
Frost wedging needs the freeze-thaw cycle (temperature going above and below 0 C again and again), not just cold. Rock frozen all year long does not wedge much.

steps.title: Frost wedging
bullets: Water is odd: when it freezes it **expands** (the molecules move apart to fit the ice crystal pattern), so ice is less dense than liquid water and floats. Water is densest at about 4 C.
In the picture, water in the cracks freezes and expands, so a crack grows and a block is lifted and pushed out.

steps.title: Why frost wedging works
bullets: Two things are needed together: water **expands** when it freezes, and Earth has **temperature swings** that give a freeze-thaw cycle.
That expansion is the reason frost wedging works, so the answer to the question in the picture is both reasons together.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: Almost every sedimentary rock is made with **water**: water breaks rock down, carries the pieces, and dissolves minerals that later crystallize.

A water molecule is **polar**: one side is slightly positive (the two hydrogens) and the other slightly negative (the oxygen), like a tiny magnet or battery. That makes water a **universal solvent**: it pries ions (charged atoms) off crystals, and given enough time it can dissolve even strong minerals.

sections.title: Physical vs chemical weathering and surface area

boxes.text: Why does smaller mean faster? Chemical weathering happens only where water touches rock. A big block has surface only on the outside. Break it into tiny cubes and every cube has its own outside. Same rock, much more surface, much faster reaction. Sugar cube vs powdered sugar in tea.
More cracks = more surface = faster rot. Volume stays the same; only surface area grows.

Textbook 5.2.2 uses different cube numbers (surface area 96, 192, 384 for 64 units of volume). Practice-midterm Q27: a 2 x 2 x 2 m block (24 m2) split into eight 1 m cubes gives 8 x 6 = 48 m2, so it doubles.

steps.title: Surface area and the granite story
bullets: The two kinds of weathering work together. Physical weathering makes cracks and new surfaces. Chemical weathering only attacks surfaces, so more surface means faster chemical weathering.
Cube picture: the same amount of rock cut into more pieces. Surface area goes **6 m2, 12 m2, 60 m2** as there are more cracks (fewer cracks = less surface area).

Granite story: intact rock (feldspar, quartz, biotite), then chemical weathering weakens it and it falls apart, **feldspar turns into clay**, quartz grains are left, and a current washes the clay away while tumbling quartz grains become **rounder**.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: **Weathering** = rock at Earth's surface breaking down into smaller pieces (sediment) and dissolved ions. **Erosion** = moving that material away.

**Physical (mechanical) weathering** breaks rock into smaller pieces; the rock is the same stuff, just in smaller bits. **Chemical weathering** changes or dissolves the minerals themselves (water, oxygen and acids react with them).

boxes.text: Why does a tree split rock? A root is alive and keeps growing. It squeezes into a tiny joint, then thickens and pushes. Slow but strong, like a crowbar that keeps pushing for years.
Wedging = a wedge pushing a crack open. Frost wedge = ice, root wedge = tree, salt wedge = salt crystal.
Salt wedging is MECHANICAL (crystals physically push), not chemical, even though it involves salt. Also: the textbook says salt wedging happens where evaporation is high or near the sea.

steps.title: Jointing
bullets: **Jointing** is natural cracks in rock. Different rock types have different joints: horizontal bedding joints and vertical joints in sandstone, **exfoliation joints** (curved sheets parallel to the surface) in granite.
**Pressure expansion** (exfoliation): rock buried deep is under high pressure. When erosion exposes it, the pressure drops suddenly, the rock expands and cracks, and layers peel off like onion skin.

steps.title: Joints limit block size
bullets: Joints limit the size of the largest lumps of intact rock, so the answer is jointing.
Joints are also the doorways that let water, ice and roots into the rock.

steps.title: Salt crystal wedging
bullets: **Salt crystal wedging**: salty water evaporates in rock pores, salt crystals grow and push the rock apart.
On a beach cliff in Scotland this makes **cavernous weathering**, a honeycomb of holes (also called **tafoni**). Salt crystals are what grow in the rock.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: **Frost wedging**: water in a crack freezes and expands, so a crack grows and a block is lifted and pushed out. **Root wedging**: a tree grows in a joint, roots pry the rock apart, and eventually the blocks tumble to the base of the cliff.

boxes.text: Why do corners round off first? A corner is hit by weathering from three sides, an edge from two, a flat face from one. More exposed sides means faster loss. After enough time the sharp block is a ball.
Quartz is the survivor: after chemical weathering of granite, feldspar becomes clay, biotite rots, but the quartz sand grains remain. Beaches full of quartz sand are what is left over.

Practice-midterm Q28 asks which mineral weathers FASTEST: the answer is olivine (top of Bowen's series), not quartz. Also do not mix up oxidation (adds oxygen to iron, makes rusty colours) with dissolution (mineral breaks into ions in water).

steps.title: Oxidation
bullets: **Oxidation**: iron in a mineral combines with oxygen, like rust. The picture shows weathered **pyrite** crystals with rusty rings around them.
Iron oxides include red or grey hematite, brown goethite and yellow limonite. They colour rock red or brown and can cement grains together.
Weathering attacks a **corner on three sides, an edge on two sides, a face on one side**. So corners wear fastest and blocks turn into rounded boulders, like this granite in the Mojave desert.
This is also called spheroidal weathering, a kind of exfoliation caused by chemical weathering moving along joints.

Minerals differ too (**Goldich dissolution series**): minerals that crystallize first at high temperature (top of **Bowen's series**: olivine, pyroxene) weather fastest. Quartz, at the bottom, is very resistant.

steps.title: Does life speed it up?
bullets: Salt (halite) and calcite dissolve easily, and slightly acidic water dissolves faster.
Lichens and bacteria release acids, so **life speeds up chemical weathering**. The answer to the question in the picture is yes.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: **Dissolution**: water molecules are polar, so they pull ions out of the crystal surface. Grain surfaces become pitted and the ions end up in solution. Water seeping into joints in limestone cuts deep troughs (limestone pavement).
**Hydrolysis**: water and carbonic acid react with silicate minerals such as feldspar and turn them into **clay** plus dissolved ions. This is the main way silicate rock is broken down.

boxes.text: Why is tropical soil mostly iron and aluminum oxides? Lots of warm rain washes (leaches) away the soluble stuff such as calcite and nutrients, and only the stubborn iron and aluminum oxides stay behind. In a desert there is little rain, so calcite is not washed out and instead builds up as calcrete.
O-A-E-B-C-R: 'Old Aunts Eat Big Cakes, Really'. Rain washes things DOWN: A/E lose material (leaching), B gains it (accumulation).
Both are fine. Do not mix leaching (removal, upper layers) with accumulation (deposit, B horizon).

steps.title: How soil forms and its layers
bullets: Rain enters the ground, plant debris builds up, worms churn it, microbes and fungi work, roots weather minerals, and downward-moving water carries ions and clay from the **zone of leaching** (top) to the **zone of accumulation** (below).

Horizons (layers), top to bottom: O (dead plant material), A (topsoil, humus plus minerals), E (leached layer in wet climates), B (subsoil, where leached material collects), C (broken-up bedrock, little chemical change), R (solid bedrock). A simpler diagram labels them topsoil, transition, subsoil, weathered bedrock, solid bedrock.

steps.title: Climate: desert, temperate, tropical
bullets: A diagram compares polar, temperate, desert and tropical soils. The **tropical** block has the thickest weathered zone and is orange (iron and aluminum oxides). A red soil like the one in the picture has the colour you would expect from iron oxide.
More rain from left to right: **desert soil** (A, B, C horizons) is where calcite accumulates to form **calcrete**.
**Temperate soil** (O, A, E, B, C): humus accumulates, iron and aluminum oxide collect in B, and calcite is leached. **Tropical soil**: iron oxide, aluminum oxide and aluminum hydroxide residue.

steps.title: Rock type, slope and time
bullets: Rock type: thicker soil forms over a **weaker** substrate; the hardest rock has no soil.
Slope: thicker soil on **gentler** slopes, exposed rock on steep ones.
Time: an **older** soil is thicker than a younger one (a young lava flow has thin soil).

steps.title: Key points
bullets: **Soil** = a mix of air, water, minerals and organic matter that forms where rock weathers and meets life. **Humus** is the dark organic part.
Soil is shaped by four factors: **climate and vegetation**, substrate composition, slope steepness and wetness, and **time**.

boxes.text: Why are the names a clue? Many orders end in -sol (soil) and the front says what it is: Histo (tissue, organic), Gel (frozen), Ox (oxide), Arid (dry), Ent (recent, no layers).
Ox = oxide = tropical, Arid = dry, Histo = organic swamp, Gel = frozen, Ent = just started (no horizons).
Do not memorise all orders word for word; know the ones tied to climate (Oxisol, Aridisol, Gelisol, Histosol).

steps.title: Soil orders
bullets: The US uses the **U.S. Comprehensive Soil Classification System**. It sorts soils into **soil orders**.

Orders tied to climate: Oxisol = very weathered, rich in aluminum and iron oxide, low in nutrients, tropical. Aridisol = low organic matter, carbonate horizons, arid. Histosol = organic-rich, swamps and marshes. Gelisol = permafrost.

Other orders: Andisol = volcanic ash. Entisol = no horizons, very recent. Mollisol = soft, black, nutrient-rich, grasslands. Vertisol = clay that swells when wet and cracks when dry. Alfisol = subsurface clay, humid forests. Spodosol = acidic, ashy, humid forests. Ultisol = very mature, low nutrients. Inceptisol = moist, poorly developed horizons, recent.

steps.title: Soils of the world
bullets: The world map colours each region by its soil order, so you can see where each kind of soil is common.
Oxisols (red) are mostly in tropical regions, matching their description as very weathered tropical soils.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: Quick checks: jointing limits the size of intact lumps of rock; frost wedging works because water expands on freezing and temperatures cycle across 0 C; life speeds up chemical weathering.

sections.title: What is sediment? The four rock types

boxes.text: Why is the cover thin? Sedimentary rocks only form at the surface from weathered bits, so they sit as a skin on top of the older rock below. In the Grand Canyon you can see the layered cover sitting on basement.
Clastic = clasts (broken bits). Bio = shells. Chemical = crystals out of water. Organic = carbon (coal).

Not a sedimentary rock type: felsic or mafic (those describe igneous rocks). Biochemical vs organic: biochemical = animals built shells from dissolved minerals; organic = carbon-rich remains such as plant matter and coal. Practice: midterm Q14 answer is 'mafic'. Textbook 5.3 groups sedimentary rocks into just two big classes (clastic and chemical), with biochemical and organic sorted under chemical.

steps.title: Layers record Earth's history
bullets: Sedimentary rocks form layers like pages in a stack. The layers record ancient events and ancient environments, and geologists can read this history. The Grand Canyon is a famous example.
Sedimentary rocks are **usually a thin cover** over older **basement** rock (a diagram labels Layer, Cover and Basement). The grains and the cement preserve evidence of how the rock formed.
There are four types: clastic, biochemical, organic and chemical.

**Clastic**: loose rock fragments (**clasts**) cemented together. Biochemical: cemented shells of organisms. Chemical: minerals that crystallize directly from water. Organic: carbon-rich remains of once-living organisms (coal).
Weathering supplies the raw materials: **particles** (for clastic) and **dissolved ions** (for chemical and biochemical).

steps.title: Key points
bullets: **Sediment** = loose fragments of rock or minerals, shells and shell pieces, or mineral crystals that **precipitate** (crystallize) out of water. In the rock cycle, erosion, transport and deposition make sedimentary rock.

sections.title: Clastic rocks: making them and classifying them

boxes.text: Why do angular clasts mean 'close to home'? A broken rock has sharp corners. Rubbing and bouncing along a river or beach knocks corners off. Sharp corners left means it did not travel far; very round and well sorted means a long trip.
BReccia = BRoken, angular. COnglomerate = rounded COBBLES. Shale is Sheets (fissile).
Clast COLOUR is not used to classify clastic rocks (midterm Q13). Sorting is about size range, rounding is about corners; sphericity (roundness of shape) is a different thing from rounding.

Clue
rows: Rounded vs angular vs large clasts in mud

steps.title: A clastic rock: sandstone
bullets: A clastic rock is made of grains (**clasts**) cemented together. The picture shows a sandstone layer in a cliff, and the circle zooms in on the sand grains.

steps.title: Making a clastic rock
bullets: Weathering breaks rock, erosion carries it, **deposition** drops it. Coarse grains drop near the source, fine grains travel farther.

**Lithification** = loose sediment turns to rock. The weight of overburden causes **compaction** (squeezes grains, water escapes). Groundwater ions then cement the grains together (calcite, silica or iron oxides as cement).

steps.title: Sorting
bullets: **Sorting** has five levels: very poorly, poorly, moderately, well and very well sorted. Well sorted = grains about the same size; poorly sorted = mixed sizes.
Wind and beach sands are well sorted; glacial deposits are very poorly sorted.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: **Angularity**: grains are called angular, subangular, subrounded or rounded. Grains round off as they tumble, so more rounded means longer transport or more energy.

**Grain size**: > 2 mm is coarse: conglomerate (rounded), **breccia** (angular), diamictite (large clasts in a muddy matrix). 0.07 to 2 mm: sandstone (quartz sandstone, arkose, lithic sandstone, wacke). 0.004 to 0.06 mm: siltstone. < 0.004 mm: shale (breaks into platy sheets) or mudstone (does not).

boxes.text: Why do evaporites form? Water carries dissolved salts. When the water evaporates, the salts have nowhere to go and crystallize. Order as seawater evaporates: calcite first (about 50% of the water left), gypsum or anhydrite (20%), halite (10%), potassium and magnesium salts last (5%). Least soluble comes out first.
Limestone = LIFE (shells and reefs). Evaporite = EVAPORATION. Travertine = caves and hot springs.
Both are true: silica shells = biochemical chert, silica out of groundwater = chemical chert.

steps.title: Biochemical limestone
bullets: **Biochemical limestone** is built from shells and reefs. The mineral is mainly **calcite** (CaCO3). Shells start as aragonite (same formula, different crystal structure), which usually turns to calcite.
Limestone is the most common non-clastic sedimentary rock.

steps.title: Biochemical chert
bullets: **Biochemical chert** comes from tiny silica shells (radiolarians, diatoms) that settle on the deep ocean floor.

steps.title: Organic: coal and oil shale
bullets: **Organic** rocks are the carbon-rich remains of life: **coal and oil shale**. Plant and animal remains that are buried and heated become coal, oil and natural gas.
The picture shows a black coal layer sitting between layers of sandstone and shale.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: **Chemical evaporites**: salts that crystallize as water evaporates in dry places (a Death Valley salt flat is an example). Examples are halite and gypsum.
**Chemical travertine**: calcite from springs and in caves (stalactites). **Chemical chert**: silica from groundwater, with growth rings visible (agate and jasper are chert varieties).

boxes.text: Why is a graded bed coarse at the bottom? In a turbidity current the water is churning and carries everything. As it slows, the heaviest pebbles settle first, then sand, then silt and mud. Like shaking a jar of mixed soil and letting it sit: stones at the bottom, mud on top.
Cross beds are frozen avalanches of sand on the steep slip face. The steep side points the way the current went.

Ripples form perpendicular to flow. Midterm Q15: bedforms are structures formed in sediment during and soon after deposition. If a graded bed is coarse on TOP, the beds may be upside down (up-direction indicators, textbook 5.4.9).

steps.title: Bedforms are clues
bullets: Sedimentary structures (bedforms) are clues to the **depositional environment**. Water flowing over loose sediment creates bedforms that reflect flow speed and grain size.
**Ripple marks**: cm-scale ridges and troughs, perpendicular to flow, in sand. **Dunes**: bigger versions (50 cm to over 100 m) in streams, deserts and beaches.
Dunes preserve large internal **cross beds**.

steps.title: Cross beds
bullets: Sand moves up the gentle side of a ripple or dune and piles at the crest, then slips down the steep **slip face**. The slip face moves downcurrent and gets buried by the next avalanche; the buried slip faces are the **cross beds**.

steps.title: Turbidity currents and graded beds
bullets: Sediment breaks loose and avalanches down a submarine canyon, then slows and deposits on a submarine fan.
A **graded bed** is **coarse at the base and fine at the top** because the turbulence dies down over time.

steps.title: Mudcracks and footprints
bullets: **Mudcracks** are polygonal drying cracks in wet mud. They show alternating wet and dry **terrestrial** conditions.
**Fossil footprints** show past life. Bed-surface markings like these form after deposition while the sediment is still soft.

steps.title: A bed may have bedforms
bullets: A sedimentary bed may have **bedforms**: structures such as ripples, dunes, cross beds and mudcracks.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: **Bedding**: layers are called **beds**. Reddish sandstones and shales (redbeds) often show horizontal bedding. Each bedding plane is a change in deposition conditions; a bed is thicker than 1 cm, a thinner layer is a lamina.

**Formations**: distinct rock units so recognizable they can be mapped over large regions. They are named for places where they are best exposed. Grand Canyon example: Kaibab Limestone, Toroweap Formation, Coconino Sandstone, Hermit Shale, Supai Group. The surface between two units is a **contact**.

boxes.text: Why does a river build a delta? A river on land is fast and can carry lots. When it enters the sea or a lake the slope drops to zero, the water slows, and it dumps its load: coarse first, then finer farther out.
TFB: Top, Fore, Bottom sets. Top is flat gravel, Fore slopes down the front, Bottom is flat fine mud at the base.
Reefs need clear water (textbook: silt and clay hurt coral growth). Mudcracks mean exposure to air, so they point to tidal flats or floodplains, not deep water.

steps.title: A delta on Mars
bullets: A **delta** forms where a river slows as it meets the sea, so its sediment drops.
The picture shows a delta in Jezero crater on Mars, so water once flowed there.

steps.title: Delta layers: top, fore, bottom
bullets: A delta has topset beds (gravel, nearly horizontal), foreset beds (gravel and sand, sloping), and bottomset beds (finer sediment, horizontal). Kodiak Butte, a delta remnant, shows all three.
Around a delta you also find river-mouth sand, marsh mud, submarine mudflows and turbidites.

steps.title: Shallow-water carbonate
bullets: Shallow-water carbonate settings have a **reef**, a lagoon, calcite sand and calcite mud, and a reef face with broken reef fragments.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: A **depositional environment** is a place where sediment accumulates. They range from terrestrial to coastal to marine. Each differs in energy, transport and chemistry, so each makes its own rock.

Glacial, desert, lake, river, beach, delta, reef, submarine fan and deep-sea settings each produce different rocks (shale, siltstone, sandstone, conglomerate, limestone). A **river** leaves channel fill and floodplain deposits (older and younger).

boxes.text: Why does sand under shale under limestone mean the sea rose? Near the shore the water is shallow and energetic, so sand collects. Farther out and deeper, quieter water drops mud, and farther still, limestone. If sea level rises, the shore moves inland and deeper-water rocks pile on top of the shallow ones. So coarse (sandstone) to fine to limestone going UP = transgression.
TRANSgression = the sea TRANSports the shore inland (deeper up). REGression = the sea RETreats (shallower up, erosion).
Do not confuse 'basement' (older rock below) with 'basin' (a low place where sediment collects). Regression does not mean deposition stops; it means land is exposed and erosion increases.

head: Basin
How it forms
rows: Weight of a mountain belt pushes the crust down
Downward slip on faults makes narrow troughs
Forms in a continent's interior, maybe over an old rift
Subsidence over thinned crust at an ocean edge

steps.title: Four basin types
bullets: **Foreland** (weight of a mountain belt pushes down the crust), **rift** (downward slip on faults makes narrow troughs), intracontinental (forms in a continent's interior, maybe over an old rift), passive margin (subsidence over thinned crust at an ocean edge).
**Passive margins** are continent edges that are not plate boundaries, with continental crust thinned by earlier rifting that passes into oceanic crust.

steps.title: Transgression and regression
bullets: Sea level rise moves the shoreline inland (**transgression**); sea level fall moves it seaward (**regression**). Regression exposes land and increases erosion.
Strata record **deepening or shallowing upward** as vertical successions.
**Facies**: rocks of the same age can differ sideways (beach sand, tidal flat silt, offshore mud, offshore limestone). During transgression, beach facies get buried by offshore facies.
Grand Canyon example: Tapeats Sandstone (beach), Bright Angel Shale (near-offshore mud), Muav Limestone (far offshore).

steps.title: Foreland basins
bullets: **Foreland basins** lie on the craton side of a collisional mountain belt. The lithosphere flexes under the load, and the downwarp fills with debris eroded from the mountains.
Calgary is just east of the Rocky Mountains, so it sits on a foreland basin.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: **Sedimentary basins** form where tectonic activity creates space. Sediment thickness varies from zero to **20+ km**.
**Basement vs cover**: sedimentary rock is a cover over older **basement** rock, and what underlies the sedimentary cover is the basement.

cards.back: The breakdown of rock at Earth's surface into smaller pieces (sediment) and dissolved ions. Erosion then moves the pieces away.
Breaks rock into smaller pieces without changing the minerals. Examples: jointing, frost, root and salt wedging.
Minerals are changed or dissolved by water, oxygen and acids: dissolution, oxidation, hydrolysis. Strongest in warm, humid climates.
Cutting a rock into more pieces raises total surface area (for example 6, 12, then 60 m2), so chemical weathering is faster. Volume stays the same.
Natural cracks in rock (bedding, vertical and exfoliation joints). Jointing limits the size of the largest intact lumps and lets water, ice and roots in.
Water in a crack freezes and expands, widening the crack. Needs a freeze-thaw cycle, so temperatures must swing above and below 0 C.
A tree root grows in a joint and pries the rock apart until blocks tumble down the cliff.
Salt crystals grow in rock pores as water evaporates and push the rock apart, giving cavernous weathering (tafoni) such as a beach cliff in Scotland.
cards.short: Growing salt crystals make honeycomb holes

cards.back: Polar water molecules pull ions from a crystal surface into solution. Makes pitted grains and limestone troughs and caves.
Iron in minerals combines with oxygen (rusting). Forms hematite, goethite, limonite. Example: weathered pyrite.
Acidic water reacts with silicate minerals such as feldspar and turns them into clay plus dissolved ions.
cards.short: Feldspar plus acid water gives clay

cards.back: Corners are attacked on 3 sides, edges on 2, faces on 1, so corners wear fastest and blocks become rounded boulders.
Weathering rate follows Bowen's series: olivine and pyroxene (top, form hot) weather fastest; quartz (bottom) is very resistant.
Soil is air, water, minerals and organic matter where weathered rock meets life. Humus is the organic part.
O (plant litter), A (topsoil), E (leached), B (subsoil, accumulation), C (broken bedrock), R (solid bedrock). Leaching removes material in upper layers; B is the zone of accumulation.
cards.short: O, A, E, B, C, R layers

cards.back: Climate and vegetation, substrate composition, slope steepness and wetness, and time.
Low rainfall. Calcite accumulates to form calcrete. Horizons A, B, C.
Highest rainfall: very thick, red/orange, iron oxide, aluminum oxide and aluminum hydroxide residue, low in nutrients.
cards.short: Thick red iron and aluminum oxide soil

cards.back: Clastic, biochemical, organic and chemical. Weathering supplies particles and dissolved ions for all of them. 'Mafic' and 'felsic' are not types.
Loose rock fragments (clasts) cemented together. Classified by grain size, angularity and sorting, not colour.
Cemented shells of organisms, mainly calcite (limestone). Living things pull dissolved minerals out of water.
Minerals that crystallize directly from water, usually by evaporation. Examples: evaporites (halite, gypsum), travertine, chert.
Carbon-rich remains of once-living organisms, such as coal and oil shale.
Sediment turns to rock: burial weight compacts grains and drives out water, then ions in groundwater cement them together.
Grains go angular, subangular, subrounded, rounded as they travel and abrade. Rounder means longer transport or more energy.
How similar the grain sizes are: very poorly to very well sorted. Wind and beach sands are well sorted; glacial deposits are poorly sorted.
cards.short: Spread of grain sizes in a rock

cards.back: Over 2 mm: conglomerate, breccia, diamictite. 0.07 to 2 mm: sandstone. 0.004 to 0.06 mm: siltstone. Under 0.004 mm: shale (platy) or mudstone.
cards.short: Gravel, sand, silt, clay size ladder

cards.back: Both have clasts over 2 mm. Breccia has angular clasts (close to source); conglomerate has rounded pebbles and cobbles.
Limestone is mostly calcite from shells and reefs (aragonite shells revert to calcite). Biogenic chert is silica from tiny shells such as diatoms.
cards.short: Calcite shells; silica shells make chert

cards.back: Evaporites: salts left as water evaporates. Order as seawater evaporates: calcite, gypsum, halite, then K and Mg salts. Travertine: calcite from springs and caves.
Beds are the layers of a sedimentary rock. A formation is a rock unit distinctive enough to map over large regions, named for where it is best exposed.
Both are bedforms made by flowing water or wind. Ripples are cm-scale ridges perpendicular to flow; dunes are much larger versions.
Made by ripple and dune migration: sand slips down the steep slip face, which is buried by the next avalanche and preserved as inclined layers.
cards.short: Buried slip faces of migrating dunes

cards.back: A turbidity current slows and drops coarse sediment first, then finer, so each bed is coarse at the base and fine at the top.
cards.short: Coarse base grading to fine top

cards.back: Polygonal drying cracks in wet mud. They show alternating wet and dry terrestrial conditions.
Topset beds (gravel, nearly horizontal), foreset beds (gravel and sand, sloping), bottomset beds (fine sediment, horizontal).
Foreland (mountain weight pushes crust down), rift (fault troughs), intracontinental (interior), passive margin (subsidence over thinned crust).
Transgression: sea level rises, shoreline moves inland, deeper rocks bury shallow ones. Regression: sea level falls, shoreline moves seaward, land is exposed and eroded.
cards.short: Rising sea inland; falling sea seaward

cards.back: Rock of the same age can differ sideways because different environments existed at once (beach sand, offshore mud, limestone). Facies reflect depositional environment.
cards.short: Sideways rock differences in one age

cards.back: Sedimentary rock is often a thin cover over older basement rock below it.

quiz.q: After a granite has undergone intense chemical weathering, what mineral would most of the remaining sand grains be?
quiz.why: Feldspar turns into clay and biotite breaks down, but quartz is very resistant, so quartz grains are left. Clay is far too fine to be sand.

quiz.q:
Frost wedging is possible as a mechanical weathering agent because:
(a) water has a low density
(b) water expands when it freezes
(c) water contracts when it freezes
(d) Earth has temperature variations resulting in a freeze-thaw cycle
quiz.why: Ice takes up more room than water, and the temperature must cross 0 C again and again so the water freezes, melts and refills the widening crack.

quiz.q: A 2 m x 2 m x 2 m block of rock is split into eight 1 m cubes. How does its total surface area change?
quiz.why: The big block has 6 faces of 4 m2 = 24 m2. Each 1 m cube has 6 x 1 = 6 m2, and 8 cubes give 48 m2. Same volume, double the surface, so chemical weathering is faster.

quiz.q: Which mineral weathers fastest at Earth's surface?
quiz.why: Minerals that crystallize first at high temperature (top of Bowen's series, such as olivine) weather fastest. Quartz is at the bottom and is the most resistant.

quiz.q:
Which of these are mechanical weathering? I. Frost wedging
II. Oxidation
III. Root wedging
quiz.why: Frost wedging and root wedging physically pry rock apart. Oxidation (iron plus oxygen) changes the mineral, so it is chemical weathering.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the four soil-forming factors?
quiz.why: The four soil-forming factors are climate and vegetation, substrate composition, slope steepness and wetness, and time.

quiz.q: A soil profile is very thick, deep red, and its B horizon contains mostly iron and aluminum oxides. What climate formed it?
options: Any climate, if given enough time
quiz.why: Heavy rain leaches away soluble material and leaves iron and aluminum oxide residue. Tropical soil and the Oxisol description say exactly this.

quiz.q: Where is chemical weathering usually the DOMINANT weathering process?
options: Ground that is frozen all year
quiz.why: Chemical reactions need water and heat. Higher temperatures speed them up, and humid places supply plenty of water.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT used in classifying clastic sedimentary rocks?
quiz.why: Clastic rocks are classified by clast size, angularity (rounding), sorting and composition. Colour is not a classification criterion.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the four types of sedimentary rocks?
quiz.why: The four types are clastic, biochemical, organic and chemical. Mafic describes igneous rock composition.

quiz.q: A sandstone is made of well-sorted, well-rounded quartz grains. What does this suggest?
options: Short transport from a nearby source
Long transport and reworking, as on a beach or desert dunes
quiz.why: Rounding means grains were worn during a long trip or energetic transport, and wind and beach sands are very well sorted. Glacial deposits are poorly sorted.

quiz.q: A rock contains angular, centimetre-sized clasts in a poorly sorted mix. What is it most likely?
options: Conglomerate, deposited far from its source
Breccia, deposited close to its source
Quartz sandstone, deposited on a beach
quiz.why: Clasts over 2 mm that are angular make a breccia. Sharp corners mean the grains did not travel far.

quiz.q: In a turbidite graded bed, the grains are coarsest at the TOP. What does this most likely mean?
options: The bed has been turned upside down (overturned) by deformation
The current got stronger over time
It is a chemical sedimentary rock
quiz.why: A normal turbidite is coarse at the base and fine at the top because the current slows. Coarse on top is a clue the layers may be upside down. (Another process could cause it; the usual pattern is normal grading, coarse at the base.)

quiz.q: Thick layers of halite and gypsum in a rock sequence indicate that the area was once:
options: A coral reef in clear tropical water
A restricted basin or lake where evaporation exceeded water input
quiz.why: Halite and gypsum are evaporites: salts left when water evaporates faster than it is replaced.

quiz.q: In a vertical sequence going upward, sandstone is overlain by shale, which is overlain by limestone. What does this record?
quiz.why: Beach sand is shallow, mud lies farther offshore, and limestone farther still. Deeper-water rock on top means the shoreline moved inland as sea level rose.

quiz.q: How do cross beds form?
options: Ripples or dunes migrate downcurrent; sand moves down the steep slope of the dune and each slip face is buried by the next avalanche
Mud settles slowly from still water
Wet mud dries and shrinks into polygons
quiz.why: The buried slip faces of migrating ripples and dunes are the inclined layers called cross beds.

quiz.q: The most common mineral making up the fossils in biochemical sedimentary rocks is:
quiz.why: Limestone is mostly calcite built from shells and reefs. Shells start as aragonite (same formula) and usually revert to calcite. Travertine is a rock, not a mineral.

quiz.q: What underlies the sedimentary cover of a continent?
quiz.why: Sedimentary rock is a thin cover over older basement rock (labelled Layer, Cover, Basement in the diagram).

quiz.q: In a delta, which beds slope downstream and collect gravel and sand?
quiz.why: Topsets are nearly horizontal gravel, foresets are the sloping gravel and sand, and bottomsets are horizontal fine sediment.

quiz.q: Which of these statements are correct? I. Regression results in subaerial exposure and an increased tendency for erosion. II. Transgression moves the shoreline seaward. III. Sedimentary strata can record deepening or shallowing upward.
quiz.why: Transgression moves the shore inland, so statement II is false. Regression exposes land to erosion and strata record both deepening and shallowing.

quiz.q: Polygonal cracks are preserved in a layer of ancient mud. What does this tell you about the mud?
options: It was deposited in the deep ocean basin
It was deposited by a turbidity current
It was frozen solid under a glacier
It was wet and later dried out, so it was alternately covered and exposed to air
quiz.why: Mudcracks are desiccation (drying) features and indicate alternate wet and dry terrestrial conditions.

quiz.q: As seawater evaporates, which mineral precipitates FIRST?
options: They all precipitate at the same moment
quiz.why: The order is calcite (about 50% of seawater left), gypsum or anhydrite (20%), halite (10%), then potassium and magnesium salts (5%). The least soluble precipitate first.

quiz.q: Which statements about lithification are correct? I. Compaction squeezes grains together and drives out water. II. Cementation glues grains using minerals such as calcite, silica or iron oxide. III. Lithification requires the sediment to melt.
quiz.why: Lithification is burial compaction plus cementation, not melting. Melting would make an igneous rock.

quiz.q: A deposit contains boulders, pebbles, sand and mud all mixed together. Which environment fits best?
quiz.why: Glacial deposits are the most poorly sorted sediments in nature. Wind and beach sands are very well sorted, and lagoons and the deep sea hold fine sediment.

quiz.q: Two patches of the same rock type: one on a gentle slope and one on a steep cliff. Which has thicker soil and why?
options: The steep cliff, because gravity piles soil up on it
Both are the same because the rock is the same
The steep cliff, because rain is heavier there
Neither forms soil; soil only forms on lava
The gentle slope, because soil stays in place instead of washing or falling away
quiz.why: Thicker soil develops over gentler slopes. Steep slopes shed soil and leave exposed rock.
